item.title: We need a word for
item.description:
• We need a word for the revulsion that an artist feels when they iterate over a piece of art to perfect it, but in that painstakingly repetitive process, their own work, the offspring that they had great love for in conceiving it, starts to feel mechanical, academic and devoid of any beauty or any emotions, besides of course, disgust and a sickening feeling. Oct 12, 2026

  • We need a word for the predicament that every artist suffers in having to decide between creating art that appeals to the masses, which imposes many a constraint on the work, often uninteresting ones the artist themselves doesn’t enjoy for they find it dilutes their work, versus creating art that is free of external constraints, and comes purely out of the artists’ own decisions and self-imposed constraints, ultimately only appealing to niche corners of the public, or even just only the artist themselves, thereby raising the doubt of whether the work is even a piece of art if no mind besides that of the creator can appreciate it. Oct 12, 2026

  • We need a word for the act of observing the behavior of people around you and even yourself from a distance, as if you were a scientist with no emotional interest in the subjects. Call it anthropologizing. Anthropologizing involves cataloging and identifying behavioral patterns and explaining them; it involves a level of sterotyping and othering but not necessarily with bigoted intentions; it can be a part of a defense mechanism to avoid getting emotionally entangled or weighed down by a situation; it is also a form of meditation. It is also related to the tech-bro term of “NPC” which denotes the belief that some people behave as it they are run by a barebones program; however, terms like NPC-ization and stereotyping necessarily carry a derogatory undertone. They are simply one form of anthropologizing. Anthropologizing could also take the form of childlike curioisity towards a group of people or oneself. It could yield insightful, harmless or even helpful conclusions, especially when applied to one’s own identity. Apr 11, 2026

item.title: Thirsty US States
item.description:
When hiking with your date in the desert wilderness of Arizona—just the two of you, your breaths and the repetitive rhythm of your footsteps crushing the dry sand and rock beneath you—interrupt the monotony with the question, “Do you know what gives the state of Arizona its name?”. Your date will enthusiastically answer, “Being the only state overlapping all four North American deserts, Arizona must have something to do with being… arid?”

“It is actually the opposite. Its name comes most likely from a Native American name that means a small spring.”

Upon hearing this, your date will drop to his knees onto the rough desert floor behind you and declare, “Your etymological tales… they make me suffer a strange thirst no water can quench…” As he then starts to shed his clothes, you must continue, your eyes, lit by the brilliant sunset, scanning the horizon behind him, “The same is also true of the driest state of Nevada, whose name refers to water of a different form: Nevado in Spanish means snowy.”

An agony will now descend upon your companion. He will now proceed to grab his own throat and exclaim: “This thirst… My god! What forbidden thirst torments my flesh in this divine landscape, while this heartless enchanter in front of me weaves tales about the provenance of words, trapping me in this wretched state? Is this a mirage? A dream? Is this real?”

“You know what’s not real, pretty boy? The state of Idaho. The name, a hoax fabricated by a mining lobbyist who passed it off as a Native American word. Even worse, the name was proposed for what is now Colorado. But right when the Senate passed a bill naming Colorado ‘Idaho’, the lie was exposed, and the name dropped in favor ‘Colorado’. But the name Idaho had by then already found its way to a steamboat in the Pacific Northwest, a vessel that took gold-thirsty men along the Columbia River to inland mines, mines which came to be known as the Idaho mines in a state that later adopted the name Idaho. In the meantime, a mining town in Colorado had also already blissfully assumed the fabricated name, which explains the city of Idaho Springs in Colorado. Idaho is to state names what rectangles are to state shapes: fabrications of a settler-colonizer who wants to make his gluttonous dreams seem real.”

Now as you watch your date turn red overwhelmed by heat and thirst, you must finally turn your eyes to him and ask, unflinchingly, “Tell me. What four states in the US have names that connect to the color of the handsome thirst-stricken face in front of me?” When he says “I… don’t… know”, you’ll say “That’s a shame. Good bye. I have to go now. I pray you’re eventually relieved of the thirst you whine about.”

item.title: St Pancras International and Manchester
item.description:
The next time you’re in flirtatious contact with a pansexual partner who loves public transport, try saying, “I need to share something. Do you know what connects pansexuality, the King’s Cross Saint Pancras tube station in London and the Pancreas?” and when they say, “I don’t. But do you know [insert first name], your spontaneity—it is what makes you incredibly attractive? But tell me. What is it? What’s the answer?” you say, “The answer? That’s all.” Now when they say, “Huh? That’s all? Your riddles, your cryptic ways! They make me intensely ho-” you say, “I mean, the answer is ‘All’, the prefix “Pan-” means ‘all’ not just in ‘pansexual’, but also in Pan-cras, which means an ‘all powerful and almighty’ saint and also unexpectedly, even in Pan-creas, the ‘all flesh’ fleshy organ.”

At this point, an irrepressible ravenous desire will take hold of your partner’s heart making them writhe and heave and pant, which is when you quickly interject, “I still need to get something off my chest. Let us therefore address the chest area.” and they will most likely stare right into your eye and say the words, “Your sterile and dispassionate reference to human anatomy, it fuels my carnal appetite for you.” to which you clarify, “I mean, let’s talk about the City of Manchester. Do you know that its name likely finds its root in the chest area?”

“That appears obvious but you, my enigmatic prince, my man of deception, my man of bait and switch are never that obvious.”

“That’s right. The chest in Manchester lies not in the ‘chest’, but actually in the ‘man’ coming from an old prefix “mamm-” possibly referring to what the City of Manchester lies on: a hill that they thought resembles a…” which is exactly when your partner will interrupt, “Enough [insert full name]! We must [insert verb] right here, right now!”

item.title: What would happen if the earth were to stop rotating and revolving?
item.description:
When such a tremendous event strikes, many bizarre first-order and second-order effects will come into play, especially because of physics—–and also because of the society—, so I have carefully analyzed this hypothetical from many angles to construct the essay beneath.

First and foremost, besides everyone dying (due to physics), the clocks will stop running, both digital and analog, and also nearly all sundials, which means, the times as we know it will cease to exist. As if that shock was not enough, in its aftermath, timezones will collapse; sounds terrifying, but sociologically, it will be viewed as a great relief by two societies: US civilians who cannot tell which way the clock rotates with daylight saving time, and the grammar officials who cannot stand anyone calling it “daylight savings”.

Now, assuming no one dies so that we have more to critically study, critique and articulate on our plate, observe that many nations will be stuck in forever-day and many others in forever-night. This will inflict unprecedented disorientation upon everybody’s biology clock and cicada rhythm. But the sliver lining: the few hundreds populating the poles will do just fine as they have been enduring such fates in alternation since 0AD, so biologically speaking, it’s just a Tuesday or an August for them. More fortunately, the Antarticians are an ensemble of science experts in laboratories, which means they saw this all coming with their telescopes and their periscopes and so, were pre-prepared; and thankfully nobody is on the Arctic because it’s all thawed now.

If we refocus our analysis onto the societological rather than the scientological effects, we are faced with the eye-opening fact that one half of the global sphere will no longer need to wake up for work. Ironically, this will be a wake-up call for the national leaders (the prime ministers and the presidents and the oil and AI company executives) who will call and discuss this dire situation at once in the Alps or Versailles; they will cooperate in a mutually beneficial manner and reach an agreement that masterfully steers the economy and the planet it subsists upon, preventing in one hemisphere a recession, and on the other hemisphere, whatever is the opposite of a recession, which is either inflation or GDP. This sort of econometrics is beyond the scope of this essay, so the reader must tread here with caution.

A question must be really bothering the keen reader at this point: what happens to the solar eclipses? They will continue to happen—but only for the working people in Day Nation, which will of course be rewarding for the Day persons, assuming the Day Billionaires deem it okay for the workerly class to take a break from work—this may well be part of the economic treaty aforementioned. On the other hemisphere, the Night persons must be content with the boring Lunar eclipse, but the Night persons are fortunately mostly asleep.

What’s really depressing though about the Night nations is their plants (or “flora”, which is how good writing refers to it): the Night nation florae will all perish (biologically speaking) except for the “zz” plant which multiple plant shop owners have advised and advertised as apt for “part to no light” conditions. This too lies out of scope for this essay for the reason that I don’t own a plant shop.

But let me terminate this essay with an optimism: this is all actually exciting for the planet because there becomes possible a new form of tourism where the Night people who are unable to sleep (hopefully enough of them, from all the terror and trauma) will take planes and yachts to visit Day nations and gawk at their lush green floras and their foliages (i.e., the literary version of leaves) and vice versa. This, and the many other anti-recession opportunities that I can envision, will be enshrined in the The First Economic Treaty of the Day-Night Hemispheres, which should last at least a “day” before The First Day-Night war to end all wars breaks out and everyone dies.

item.title: Voluptuous and volume
item.description:
The next time you’re on a date and silence descends upon the table, consider blurting “Here’s a fun fact, handsome! Were you aware that the word voluptuous, in the sense of ‘a full and curvaceously attractive body’ has nothing to do with the word ‘volume’ or size? Volup in Latin means ‘with pleasure’ and ‘voluptuous’ used to qualify luxurious and pleasure-giving art, music and food.”

Now, when your date jumps from his seat, reaches across the table, holds you by your collar and tugs your face precariously close to his and exclaims in the middle of the restaurant, “My god, pretty boy, what grave injustice it is to call your facts fun! They are in fact voluptuous as fuck for me, let me prove it to you at once!” , you say “Shh! VOLUME!”, and then as he settles back into the seat in embarrassment, sweat starting to glisten at the pores of his veiny temples, he says in lowered voice “Sorry I got carried away for a moment! Where were we?”, then you say “Volume. The word volume itself comes from volvere which means to roll or twist, just like the words revolve, evolve and revolt do; volumen first referred to scrolls that had to be rolled, but as scrolls were replaced by books, ‘volume’ shifted in meaning to books, but with time, it once again shifted, this time to the thickness and bulkiness and heaviness of the books themselves or… of just about any object…”—he adjusts his tie—“then it shifted to the precise magnitude of occupied space, and then also to the magnitude of sound. Speaking of sound, how about we gently hold each others’ bodies, and turn and roll and revolve in pleasure…”—he adjusts his tie once again—“…to the mellow sound of music, and if yes, what word of similar but Germanic not Latin roots would that dance go by?”

item.title: Bridges of America
item.description: If you’re ever stuck not knowing what to say at a social gathering, how about “hello there, did you know that the phrase ‘I have a bridge to sell you’ comes from a man literally duping immigrants into buying ownership of the Brooklyn Bridge?’ and if they say “wow I’m so intrigued, tell me more bridge facts, you’re so sexy when you do that”, you can say “alrighty! did you know that the Golden in Golden Gate bridge comes from the name of the strait it is on, which was in turn named after the water inlet called Golden Horn in Instanbul attached to the Bosphorous strait which by the way is Greek for whatever the word ‘Oxford’ means?”

item.title: I did a performance on the metro.
item.description:
On the metro back from work, just as I was preparing to make my nonchalant and mysterious exit, the train decided to make an abrupt halt (#whimsical #whimsy). A jolt of unprecedented magnitude shook my being. In panic, I reached out for the nearest hanging strap. (At that instant, somewhere, at some undisclosed location, I was sure, a howling cyclone fell silent; the fronds of coconut trees ceased all flailing; violent waves and blinding lightnings froze in place. In that cosmic stillness (sourced from Tamil cinema), a stray electrical impulse materialized in my brain. It zipped a circuitous way through my synapses. It reached my pupils and dilated them with a realization:) “Fuck!”.

From the platform, my soul witnessed a magnificent painting: a man pining for a strap descending from the divine ceiling, but the strap, he would stop short of attaining. When animation returns, his body becomes toy to the laws of physics: 1) a Newtonian force clasps the spine and yanks it; 2) the torso is flung into a “C”; 3) the C rotates and falls on its butt; 4) the angular jolt sends the feet into air; 5) a second Newtonian force—the train did a second whimsical jolt of whimsy—grabs the body by its thighs and yanks it too; 6) the “C” is now an “O”; 7) the “O”, gathering momentum, makes one smooth, full rotation. A second rotation may or may not have transpired. It is a blur.

In summary, a man, dressed nicely (wearing a notably sleek backpack), signalling a docile, social-norm-abiding metropolitan lifestyle, has, out of nowhere, without making a fuss or leaving so much as a hint, just stood up and whipped out a beautiful somersault (maybe two?) in the middle of a busy San Francisco metro train at 3:45pm, all lasting a total of 2 seconds or less.

Said man now calculates. His wit must defuse the tension that has risen in the wake of his routine. Here, the universe forks into two. In one, the man says “That’s all folks! Thanks for coming to my show; tips appreciated.” and bows to his audience; the cyclone and the coconut trees resume motion. In the other, the man, reeling from being freshly assaulted by the universe, while also thrilled from his unforeseen, zero-effort demonstration of athleticism, while also noticing the aghast faces lining both sides of the runway, is disoriented from the bombardment of stimuli, exits the scene and dissolves into the stillness, mysteriously and nonchalantly.

item.title: Clouds and words
item.description: Clouds seem as if they are a flowing, gushing liquid finding their way through crevices between peaks, although at a terribly glacial pace. Yet, clouds are not fluids. As if frozen in time, barely moving, clouds appear like fluffy tufts of solid feather and cotton. Yet, clouds are not solids. What clouds are, are vapours. Yet, unlike vapours, clouds do not disperse into the atmosphere like gases must. Now, all this tells us little about how perplexing clouds are, and much about how perplexing words are: how we think words correspond to rules and defintions, but with scrutiny, this belief begins to fall apart giving way to imprecisions and exceptions, and how, despite such imprecisions and exceptions, words help us communicate our thoughts precisely.

item.title: The Curious Coincidence of Turn, Turner, Teetotum and Teetotaller
item.description:
“Dreidel” is a small Hanukkah toy, a spinning top, often made of wood. The term stems from an old German word meaning to turn, the object itself from a European gambling toy called “teetotum”. The wheels in the reader’s head now start to turn: Gambling, teetotum, the Germans… this must all lead us to alcohol and “teetotaller”, right? Turns out, not.

The toy “teetotum”, we are told, came from “t-totum”, the “t” to do with a token on the toy meaning “take it all”. Nothing to do with alcohol. The term “teetotaller”, we are told, has many competing tales, none to do with gambling.

Yet, the two seemingly unrelated terms, through sheer coincidence, become entangled. In one of the origin stories spun for “teetotaller”, a man in 1833 stammers (perhaps intentionally) when calling for “tee—tee—total abstinence”, the utterer, one Mr. Richard, surname Turner, a surname that had no part to play in coining “teetotaller”, but like its German analogs Drexel and Dreyer, at some point referred to craftsmen who made small (often wooden) objects using a lathe, thus returning us, through a fortuitous, playful and dizzying turn of symbols, back to the small Hanukkah toy, a spinning top, often made of wood termed “Dreidel”.

item.title: Gas leak and leek gas
item.description:
An army of maintenance staff, various contraptions slung across their shoulders, barged into my tiny NYC apartment alarmed by my complaint: the stove was leaking gas. Their contraptions however reported nothing. All good, bye-bye. The sun set and the sun rose and once again the ominous vapors of gas came knocking at my nostrils; once again, the army came knocking at my door, and once again, nothing.

But I was no mad man imagining things. I traced with my own superhuman snout every surface and every ridge of my kitchen, turning it inside out, turning my own lungs inside out, certain that the cuplrit would eventually graze the tip of my nose, which it did.

My apartment, I discovered, was not on the brink of an explosion. It was being lovingly fondled by the sloppy breath of garlic, periodically exhaled by a (washed) jar of garlic paste (that I had just added to my precious recycled jar collection).

But why would garlic reek of natural gas? I ran to The Computer: O, dear! What gives natural gas its odor?. The Computer said “Aye, Aye Captain, what you seek are organosulphuric additives called mercaptans!”. When did they begin doing this? In 1937, a school in Texas went up in flames taking with it the lives of hundreds of students and teachers. In a shocking turn of events, lawmakers did something to protect school students within a span of a few weeks, which was to enforce odorization of natural gas. President Roosevelt received a sympathetic telegram from er… the then leader of Germany. See photo.

Then, pray tell, from what does garlic take its smell? The Computer said “Mr. Alice-in-Wonderland, your rabbit hole has led you to the organosulfuric allicin, emitted in defense by garlic crushed.”

The link between the two I would find at the end of another rabbit hole: the oesophagus. Allicin, trapped in the stomach, breaks down into vapours of allyl mercaptan (aha!) that is released out into broad daylight as garlic breath.

Just as the case was being closed, another bulb lit up: does allyl have anything to do with the genus that garlic and its odorous, bulbous siblings (onions, leeks, shallots and chives) belong to: allium? The Computer nodded. An allyl derivative, it seems, was first extracted from garlic oil, thus obtaining that name, much like how the “but-" in “butane” comes from (rancid) butter (latin: butyrum) from which butyric acid was first derived.

Allyl’s well that end’s well?
